blocks.body:
The fraction $355/113$ agrees with $\pi$ to six decimal places, although its denominator is only $113$. A decimal approximation of the same quality, $3.141593$, needs a denominator of a million. Why does such a fraction exist, how would anyone find it, and is it the best possible for its size?

Continued fractions answer all three questions. They encode a real number as a sequence of integers obtained by repeatedly taking the integer part and inverting what is left. For rational numbers the process is exactly the [[divisibility|Euclidean algorithm]]; for irrational numbers it runs forever and produces the sequence of best rational approximations, and for square roots it becomes periodic, which is the key to [[pell|Pell's equation]].

blocks.title: The Euclidean algorithm in disguise
blocks.body:
Run the Euclidean algorithm on $43$ and $19$:

$$43 = 2 \cdot 19 + 5, \quad 19 = 3 \cdot 5 + 4, \quad 5 = 1 \cdot 4 + 1, \quad 4 = 4 \cdot 1.$$

Each line can be read as a statement about fractions: $\frac{43}{19} = 2 + \frac{5}{19} = 2 + \frac{1}{19/5}$, then $\frac{19}{5} = 3 + \frac{1}{5/4}$, and so on. Nesting them,

$$\frac{43}{19} = 2 + \cfrac{1}{3 + \cfrac{1}{1 + \cfrac{1}{4}}}.$$

We abbreviate this as $[2; 3, 1, 4]$. The entries are precisely the quotients of the Euclidean algorithm.

The same procedure makes sense for any real $\alpha$. Set $\alpha_0 = \alpha$ and repeat

$$a_k = \lfloor \alpha_k \rfloor, \qquad \alpha_{k+1} = \frac{1}{\alpha_k - a_k},$$

stopping if $\alpha_k$ is an integer. For example $\sqrt 2 = 1 + (\sqrt 2 - 1)$ and $\frac{1}{\sqrt 2 - 1} = \sqrt 2 + 1 = 2 + (\sqrt 2 - 1)$, so the same remainder recurs and $\sqrt 2 = [1; 2, 2, 2, \dots]$.

blocks.title: Simple continued fraction
blocks.body:
For an integer $a_0$ and positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots$, the finite simple continued fraction $[a_0; a_1, \dots, a_n]$ is $a_0 + 1/[a_1; a_2, \dots, a_n]$ with $[a_n] = a_n$. The infinite one $[a_0; a_1, a_2, \dots]$ is the limit of $[a_0; a_1, \dots, a_k]$ as $k \to \infty$. The numbers $a_k$ are the partial quotients, and $p_k/q_k = [a_0; a_1, \dots, a_k]$ in lowest terms is the $k$-th convergent.

The algorithm above produces an expansion of every real number. It stops if and only if $\alpha$ is rational (for rationals it is the Euclidean algorithm, which terminates; and a finite expansion is clearly rational), and for irrational $\alpha$ the convergents tend to $\alpha$, as the theorems below show.

blocks.title: Recurrence for convergents
blocks.body:
Define $p_{-2} = 0,\ p_{-1} = 1,\ q_{-2} = 1,\ q_{-1} = 0$ and, for $k \ge 0$,

$$p_k = a_k p_{k-1} + p_{k-2}, \qquad q_k = a_k q_{k-1} + q_{k-2}.$$

Then for every $k \ge 0$ and every real $x > 0$ (any real $x$ if $k = 0$),

$$[a_0; a_1, \dots, a_{k-1}, x] = \frac{x\, p_{k-1} + p_{k-2}}{x\, q_{k-1} + q_{k-2}}, \qquad\text{in particular}\qquad [a_0; \dots, a_k] = \frac{p_k}{q_k},$$

and

$$p_k q_{k-1} - p_{k-1} q_k = (-1)^{k-1}.$$

The last identity shows $\gcd(p_k, q_k) = 1$, so $p_k/q_k$ is already in lowest terms.

Induction on $k$. For $k = 0$ the left side is just $x$, and the right side is $(x \cdot 1 + 0)/(x \cdot 0 + 1) = x$.

Suppose the formula holds for $k$ (for all choices of partial quotients). Then

$$[a_0; \dots, a_{k-1}, a_k, x] = [a_0; \dots, a_{k-1}, a_k + \tfrac1x],$$

because in both expressions the innermost part is $a_k + \tfrac{1}{x}$. By the induction hypothesis with $a_k + 1/x$ in place of $x$ (allowed: it is positive when $k \ge 1$, and any real works when $k = 0$), this equals

$$\frac{(a_k + \frac1x) p_{k-1} + p_{k-2}}{(a_k + \frac1x) q_{k-1} + q_{k-2}} = \frac{p_k + \frac1x p_{k-1}}{q_k + \frac1x q_{k-1}} = \frac{x p_k + p_{k-1}}{x q_k + q_{k-1}},$$

which is the formula for $k+1$. Taking $x = a_k$ gives $[a_0; \dots, a_k] = p_k / q_k$.

For the determinant, substitute the recurrence:

$$p_k q_{k-1} - p_{k-1} q_k = (a_k p_{k-1} + p_{k-2}) q_{k-1} - p_{k-1}(a_k q_{k-1} + q_{k-2}) = -(p_{k-1} q_{k-2} - p_{k-2} q_{k-1}).$$

So the quantity changes sign at each step, and at $k = -1$ it is $p_{-1} q_{-2} - p_{-2} q_{-1} = 1$. Hence it equals $(-1)^{k-1}$. Any common divisor of $p_k$ and $q_k$ divides $\pm 1$.

blocks.title: Convergents approximate well
blocks.body:
Let $\alpha$ be irrational with convergents $p_k / q_k$. Then

$$\alpha - \frac{p_k}{q_k} = \frac{(-1)^k}{q_k\,(\alpha_{k+1} q_k + q_{k-1})}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \Bigl|\alpha - \frac{p_k}{q_k}\Bigr| < \frac{1}{q_k q_{k+1}} \le \frac{1}{q_k^2}.$$

The convergents lie alternately below ($k$ even) and above ($k$ odd) $\alpha$, and they converge to $\alpha$.

By construction $\alpha = [a_0; a_1, \dots, a_k, \alpha_{k+1}]$, so the previous theorem with $x = \alpha_{k+1}$ gives

$$\alpha = \frac{\alpha_{k+1} p_k + p_{k-1}}{\alpha_{k+1} q_k + q_{k-1}}.$$

Subtract $p_k / q_k$ and use the determinant identity:

$$\alpha - \frac{p_k}{q_k} = \frac{q_k p_{k-1} - p_k q_{k-1}}{q_k(\alpha_{k+1} q_k + q_{k-1})} = \frac{(-1)^k}{q_k(\alpha_{k+1} q_k + q_{k-1})}.$$

Since $\alpha$ is irrational, $\alpha_{k+1}$ is not an integer, so $\alpha_{k+1} > a_{k+1}$ and the denominator exceeds $q_k(a_{k+1} q_k + q_{k-1}) = q_k q_{k+1}$. Finally $q_{k+1} = a_{k+1} q_k + q_{k-1} \ge q_k$. The $q_k$ grow at least as fast as Fibonacci numbers, so the error tends to $0$.

blocks.title: Best approximations and the digits of pi
blocks.body:
The theorem says every irrational has infinitely many fractions with $|\alpha - p/q| < 1/q^2$. Much more is true; we state two classical facts without proof (proofs are in the sources listed below).

Best approximation. If $0 < q < q_{k+1}$, then $|q\alpha - p| \ge |q_k \alpha - p_k|$ for every integer $p$. So no fraction with a smaller denominator than the next convergent does better, in this strong sense, than $p_k/q_k$.

Legendre's criterion. If $|\alpha - p/q| < \dfrac{1}{2q^2}$, then $p/q$ is one of the convergents of $\alpha$.

For $\pi = [3; 7, 15, 1, 292, 1, 1, \dots]$ the recurrence gives the convergents

$$3, \quad \frac{22}{7}, \quad \frac{333}{106}, \quad \frac{355}{113}, \quad \frac{103993}{33102}, \dots$$

The error formula explains why $355/113$ is so good: its error is about $1/(q_3 \cdot q_4)$, and $q_4 = 292 \cdot 113 + 106$ is huge because the next partial quotient is $292$. Large partial quotients mean exceptionally good approximations; a number whose partial quotients stay bounded (such as $\sqrt 2$ or the golden ratio $[1; 1, 1, \dots]$) is badly approximable: there is a constant $c > 0$ with $|\alpha - p/q| > c/q^2$ for every fraction $p/q$ (see the last example below).

blocks.title: Quadratic irrationals are periodic
blocks.body:
Computing a few expansions suggests a pattern:

$$\sqrt 2 = [1; \overline{2}], \qquad \sqrt 3 = [1; \overline{1, 2}], \qquad \sqrt 7 = [2; \overline{1, 1, 1, 4}], \qquad \frac{1 + \sqrt 5}{2} = [1; \overline{1}].$$

A bar marks the repeating block. The pattern is a theorem: a real number has an eventually periodic continued fraction if and only if it is a quadratic irrational, that is, an irrational root of a quadratic equation with integer coefficients. Euler showed that periodic expansions give quadratic irrationals; the converse is Lagrange's theorem (1770).

One direction is quick. If $\alpha = [\overline{a_0; a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}}]$ is purely periodic, then $\alpha = [a_0; \dots, a_{n-1}, \alpha]$, and the recurrence theorem gives

$$\alpha = \frac{\alpha\, p_{n-1} + p_{n-2}}{\alpha\, q_{n-1} + q_{n-2}}, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad q_{n-1}\alpha^2 + (q_{n-2} - p_{n-1})\alpha - p_{n-2} = 0,$$

a quadratic equation with leading coefficient $q_{n-1} \ge 1$, and $\alpha$ is irrational because its expansion is infinite. If the expansion becomes periodic only after $j$ terms, then $\alpha = [a_0; \dots, a_{j-1}, \beta]$ with $\beta$ purely periodic, so $\alpha = (\beta p_{j-1} + p_{j-2})/(\beta q_{j-1} + q_{j-2})$. Writing $\beta = r + s\sqrt N$ with $r, s$ rational and rationalising the denominator gives $\alpha = r' + s'\sqrt N$ with $r', s'$ rational, and such an irrational number is a root of $(x - r')^2 = s'^2 N$, a quadratic equation with rational coefficients (clear denominators to make them integers). The converse takes more work: one shows that the complete quotients $\alpha_k$ of a quadratic irrational all have the shape $(m_k + \sqrt N)/d_k$ with integers $m_k, d_k$ that stay bounded, so some $\alpha_k$ must repeat.

For $\sqrt N$ with $N$ a positive integer that is not a square, the expansion has the special form $\sqrt N = [a_0; \overline{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{r-1}, 2a_0}]$, with the block before $2a_0$ a palindrome. This is what makes continued fractions solve Pell's equation.

blocks.title: A linear Diophantine equation
blocks.body: Find the continued fraction of $43/19$, list its convergents, and use them to solve $43x - 19y = 1$ in integers.
blocks.solution:
From the Euclidean algorithm, $43/19 = [2; 3, 1, 4]$. The recurrence gives

$$\begin{aligned} p_0 &= 2, & p_1 &= 3 \cdot 2 + 1 = 7, & p_2 &= 1 \cdot 7 + 2 = 9, & p_3 &= 4 \cdot 9 + 7 = 43,\\ q_0 &= 1, & q_1 &= 3 \cdot 1 + 0 = 3, & q_2 &= 1 \cdot 3 + 1 = 4, & q_3 &= 4 \cdot 4 + 3 = 19. \end{aligned}$$

So the convergents are $2, 7/3, 9/4, 43/19$. The determinant identity with $k = 3$ says $p_3 q_2 - p_2 q_3 = (-1)^2 = 1$, that is,

$$43 \cdot 4 - 9 \cdot 19 = 172 - 171 = 1.$$

So $(x, y) = (4, 9)$ is a solution, and the general solution is $x = 4 + 19t$, $y = 9 + 43t$ for $t \in \mathbb Z$. This is the same answer the extended Euclidean algorithm gives for [[bezout|Bézout's identity]]; the convergent recurrence is a tidy way to organise it.

blocks.title: The expansion of the square root of 7
blocks.body: Compute the continued fraction of $\sqrt 7$ and its first few convergents. What do you notice about $p_k^2 - 7 q_k^2$?
blocks.solution:
Since $2 < \sqrt 7 < 3$, $a_0 = 2$. Rationalising at each step:

$$\begin{aligned} \alpha_1 &= \frac{1}{\sqrt 7 - 2} = \frac{\sqrt 7 + 2}{3} \approx 1.55, & a_1 &= 1,\\ \alpha_2 &= \frac{1}{\alpha_1 - 1} = \frac{3}{\sqrt 7 - 1} = \frac{\sqrt 7 + 1}{2} \approx 1.82, & a_2 &= 1,\\ \alpha_3 &= \frac{1}{\alpha_2 - 1} = \frac{2}{\sqrt 7 - 1} = \frac{\sqrt 7 + 1}{3} \approx 1.22, & a_3 &= 1,\\ \alpha_4 &= \frac{1}{\alpha_3 - 1} = \frac{3}{\sqrt 7 - 2} = \sqrt 7 + 2 \approx 4.65, & a_4 &= 4. \end{aligned}$$

Then $\alpha_4 - 4 = \sqrt 7 - 2$, which is where we started, so $\sqrt 7 = [2; \overline{1, 1, 1, 4}]$, period $4$, ending in $2a_0 = 4$.

The convergents are $2, 3, 5/2, 8/3, 37/14, 45/17, 82/31, 127/48, \dots$, and

$$p_k^2 - 7q_k^2 = -3,\ 2,\ -3,\ 1,\ -3,\ 2,\ -3,\ 1, \dots$$

The value $1$ appears at the end of each period: $8^2 - 7 \cdot 3^2 = 1$ and $127^2 - 7 \cdot 48^2 = 1$. These are solutions of Pell's equation $x^2 - 7y^2 = 1$.

blocks.title: The square root of 2 is badly approximable
blocks.body: Prove that $\Bigl|\sqrt 2 - \dfrac pq\Bigr| > \dfrac{1}{3q^2}$ for all integers $p$ and $q \ge 1$.
blocks.solution:
If $q = 1$, the nearest integers to $\sqrt 2$ are $1$ and $2$, at distances $\sqrt 2 - 1 > 0.41$ and $2 - \sqrt 2 > 0.58$, both more than $1/3$.

Let $q \ge 2$ and suppose, for contradiction, that $|\sqrt 2 - p/q| \le 1/(3q^2) \le 1/12$. Then $p > 0$ and $p/q + \sqrt 2 \le 2\sqrt 2 + 1/12 < 2.92$. Since $\sqrt 2$ is irrational, $p^2 - 2q^2$ is a nonzero integer, so

$$\Bigl|\sqrt 2 - \frac pq\Bigr| = \frac{|p^2 - 2q^2|}{q^2\,(p/q + \sqrt 2)} \ge \frac{1}{q^2 (p/q + \sqrt 2)} > \frac{1}{2.92\, q^2} > \frac{1}{3q^2},$$

a contradiction.

So for $\sqrt 2$ the exponent $2$ in $1/q^2$ cannot be improved, and even the constant can only be improved slightly: along the convergents, $q^2 |\sqrt 2 - p/q|$ tends to $1/(2\sqrt 2) \approx 0.354$. The same argument shows every quadratic irrational is badly approximable, matching the bounded (periodic) partial quotients.

blocks.body:
- A rational number has two expansions, since $[a_0; \dots, a_n] = [a_0; \dots, a_n - 1, 1]$ when $a_n \ge 2$. The algorithm produces the one with last quotient at least $2$ (unless the number is an integer).
- Negative numbers: only $a_0$ may be negative. For instance $-1.5 = -2 + \tfrac12 = [-2; 2]$, not $[-1; 2]$.
- The inequality $|\alpha - p/q| < 1/q^2$ does not force $p/q$ to be a convergent. Legendre's criterion needs the constant $\tfrac12$.
- Computing many partial quotients in floating point is unreliable: rounding errors are amplified at each inversion. In double precision the expansion of $\pi$ already goes wrong at the fourteenth partial quotient. Use exact or high-precision arithmetic (or the integer recurrence for $\sqrt N$).

The periodic expansion of $\sqrt d$ produces the fundamental solution of [[pell|Pell's equation]] $x^2 - dy^2 = 1$, as the example with $d = 7$ already showed. The approximation theorems are the starting point of [[diophantine-approx|Diophantine approximation]]: Liouville, Thue, Siegel and Roth asked how much better than $1/q^2$ algebraic numbers can be approximated, and continued fractions give one route to irrationality: an infinite expansion with a provable pattern, such as $e = [2; 1, 2, 1, 1, 4, 1, 1, 6, \dots]$, is itself a proof that the number is irrational. Reduction of indefinite [[quadratic-forms|binary quadratic forms]] is a continued-fraction algorithm in disguise.

In dynamics, the digits are generated by the Gauss map $x \mapsto \{1/x\}$ on $(0,1)$, the fractional part of $1/x$ (see [[floor-functions]]). Gauss discovered that the measure $\dfrac{dx}{(1 + x)\ln 2}$ is invariant under this map. This leads to the Gauss–Kuzmin distribution: for almost every $\alpha$, the proportion of partial quotients equal to $k$ is $\log_2\bigl(1 + \frac{1}{k(k+2)}\bigr)$, so about $41.5\%$ of the digits are $1$.

1. Find the continued fraction of $\dfrac{1001}{365}$ and its convergents.
2. Show that $\sqrt{n^2 + 1} = [n; \overline{2n}]$ for every positive integer $n$.
3. Which number has continued fraction $[1; \overline{2, 3}]$? Find the quadratic equation it satisfies.
4. Prove that the denominators satisfy $q_k \ge F_{k+1}$, the $(k+1)$-st Fibonacci number (with $F_1 = F_2 = 1$).
